title: Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll
summary: Albertans are divided over immigration but attitudes are “softening,” while nearly half still don’t know which way they’ll vote on the nine non-separation questions in the Oct. 19 referendum, a new…

image.caption: Ballot mockups are pictured during a Sept. 3, 2026, referendum technical briefing in Edmonton. The ballots feature the questions to be presented to voters in the province's Oct. 19, 2026 referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

blocks.text: Albertans are divided over immigration but attitudes are “softening,” while nearly half still don’t know which way they’ll vote on nine non-separation questions in the Oct. 19 referendum, a new poll commissioned by CBC News suggests.

“There's a huge contrast between opinion toward question 10 (the separation question) and opinion toward the other nine,” said Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown, whose Janet Brown Opinion Research directed a random survey of 1,200 Albertans between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21.

“We really have seen a great deal of consistency over the last several months on … how people would vote for separation. You know, attitudes there are only changing slightly and very few people remain undecided about those questions.
“But the other nine, there's not a high level of familiarity with those questions … A lot is up in the air right now on the other nine questions.”
Five of those nine questions deal with immigration issues, the other four deal with changes to the Constitution.
On the immigration questions, the poll found 54 per cent of respondents agree that Alberta should take more control over immigration to the province, down three points from April.
“We're seeing that overall attitudes haven't changed very much, but those attitudes are softening,” Brown explained.
Those who “strongly agree” with the statement dropped from 40 per cent to 33 per cent, with those who “somewhat agree” increasing by four percentage points since the last poll.
“The intensity has changed, but the overall ‘agree,’ ‘disagree’ numbers haven't changed very much,” she said.

The original nine questions announced by Premier Danielle Smith in February focus on immigration policy and constitutional changes. In May, the question relating to separation was added to the ballot and has since occupied much of the discourse around the referendum.
According to the survey, 49 per cent of respondents did not yet know how they will be voting on the nine questions apart from the one on separation.
“With less than a month remaining, people aren't feeling very connected to these nine questions yet,” Brown said.

items: Albertans are voting on Oct. 19. Here’s the simple version of what you need to know

blocks.text: Immigration attitudes becoming less ‘intense’
“There is a consensus — a bare consensus — that we should take more control over immigration, but not a consensus on what that should look like,” Brown said.
The poll, carried out by Trend Research, did not put the immigration and constitutional referendum questions to respondents directly, but rather addressed larger themes.
When asked if the province should limit temporary residents’ free access to health care and education, about 45 per cent of respondents agreed.
But compared to a similar question posed in April this year, those who strongly disagreed increased by four percentage points.

Lisa Young, a professor of political science at the University of Calgary, said that as Albertans discuss the ideas on the ballot, such as the proposed policies to restrict temporary residents’ access to public services, support for those ideas seems to be decreasing.

“I think that what we've seen over the last number of weeks as people have come back from summer vacation, they've seen signs saying 'no to the nine,' for example, and they've started wondering what are the nine [questions] and engaging a little bit more around that," said Young.
The poll also asked people if, “on the whole, Alberta benefits from immigration to the province from other countries.” Sixty-three per cent of respondents said they strongly or somewhat agreed.
“That's a very strong number,” Brown said. “That's almost two-thirds of Albertans. So on balance as a province, we do feel that immigrants have a positive contribution.”

That figure is down 18 percentage points from Sept. 2021, when the same question was posed for a poll conducted for the Business Council of Alberta. But, Brown said, the context in which the question was posed is entirely different.
“It was the ‘Alberta is Calling’ era. It was the era when we were fretting about not having enough people coming to the province, having a labour shortage,” she explained.
“Fast forward to today, now that we're in a trade war, now that we're feeling like housing prices are going up, I think that accounts for the difference of opinion.”
In the past five years, Alberta’s population has grown by roughly 600,000 people. Much of that growth has been from international and interprovincial migration.

items: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: People not feeling ‘connected’ to the 9, yet

While 49 per cent of respondents say they don’t know how they will vote on the non-separation questions, 75 per cent say they will definitely cast a ballot for all nine questions, with 11 per cent suggesting they may possibly skip some questions.
Forty-four per cent of those polled said they feel either not at all familiar or not very familiar with the nine questions.

“When we look at some of these responses together, what we're seeing is that people have the intention of figuring out these questions and answering them when they go to vote, but they haven't yet done that,” Young explained.
“And it'll be interesting to see how many of them follow through once they do start trying to wade through the specifics of the questions and trying to make sense of the context for them.”
Polling data indicate that NDP voters seem to be a lot more familiar with the nine questions than UCP supporters, Brown said.

Sixty-nine per cent of respondents who identify as NDP supporters say they’re very or somewhat familiar with the nine questions, while 45 per cent of those expressing support for the UCP feel the same.

“I think that speaks to the fact that there's been a very strong ‘no to the nine’ campaign,” Brown said. “And I don't think there's been an equally strong campaign coming out of the UCP to vote yes for the nine.”

“So it seems right now that those people who are in the NDP camp — those people would vote NDP if we had an election today — they are more tuned in right now to those other nine questions, paying more attention to them than UCP supporters are.”

Only 11 per cent of UCP supporters said they will vote ‘yes’ to all nine questions, despite the province promoting this position. 61 per cent of UCP voters said they do not know yet how they will vote.
In contrast, 52 per cent of NDP supporters said they would vote ‘no’ to all nine, showing greater support for their position.

“For people who don't follow politics closely, who aren't as interested, there may be a desire to go out and vote on this one kind of existential [separation] question that I think most Albertans have got their head around one way or another at this point, but then not feel prepared to vote on the others,” Young said.
“It's going to be really interesting in the days or weeks after the [vote] to see what the differences in turnout are between question 10 and the other nine.”
Albertans head to the polls to vote on 10 questions Oct. 19.

The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.

Telephone numbers were dialed up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.
